# Tool Design as API Design {#sec-tool-design}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements run `qwen3.5:9b` through
`ollama` 0.24.0. Nothing is executed in the schema experiment — it scores the
*call* the model emits, so the model's arithmetic cannot contaminate a result
about schemas. @sec-agent-anatomy owns the loop; this chapter owns what the
loop reaches for. Software: NumPy 2.5.2 on Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- write tool schemas a model uses correctly on the first try, and say which
  part of the schema did the work;
- design error messages a model can recover from, and measure whether it does;
- decide what a tool should return, and what it must never return;
- keep a large tool surface usable, and know when to stop adding tools.

## The description is prompt text {#sec-tool-design-schema}

A [**tool schema**](#gloss-tool-schema){#term-tool-schema .term-ref} looks
like documentation and behaves like a prompt.

::: {#gloss-tool-schema .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Tool schema** — the name, description, types and enums a model sees before
choosing a call. Prompt text rather than documentation, because the model gets
one shot from it and cannot check a guess.
[↩](#term-tool-schema){.term-back}
::: That single
sentence is the chapter, and everything below is its consequences.

The distinction matters because the two are written by different instincts.
Documentation is written for a reader who can ask a colleague, read the source,
or try it and see. [A model gets one shot, from the schema alone, with no way
to check.]{.hl} It cannot open your codebase. It cannot see an example call.
Whatever the schema does not say, the model guesses — and a guess that
type-checks is indistinguishable from an understanding.

So the schema carries four separate jobs, and it is worth being able to name
which one you are doing:

| the field | the job it does |
|:--|:--|
| **name** | tells the model *when* this tool applies, before it reads anything else |
| **description** | resolves the cases the name leaves ambiguous, and rules out the ones it should not be used for |
| **parameter types and enums** | make wrong calls unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged — @sec-decoding's argument, one level up |
| **parameter descriptions** | carry the mapping from how a user phrases a thing to what your API calls it |

: Four jobs, one object {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

The last row is the one people skip, and it is where most misuse comes from.
Your users say *how much did we spend*; your API calls it `budget_allocated`.
Something has to bridge that, and if the schema does not, the model invents a
bridge.

### Measured: which part of the schema does the work?

Four versions of one tool, differing only in how they are described. The task
is to fetch one numeric field about a project, and the questions **never name
the field literally** — *how much money was allocated* has to become
`alan="butce"`. So the schema is the only thing that can carry the mapping.
Nothing is executed; what is scored is the call the model emits.

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 60 questions, one tool, four descriptions

 variant         called a tool  project right  field right  fully correct
 A. opaque               58.3%           0.0%         0.0%           0.0%
 B. named               100.0%         100.0%        25.0%          25.0%
 C. enum                100.0%         100.0%       100.0%         100.0%
 D. described           100.0%         100.0%       100.0%         100.0%
```

[The enum did all of the work.]{.hl} Going from free strings to an enumerated
list took field accuracy from **25% to 100%**, and adding careful prose
descriptions on top of that added **nothing measurable**. That is the opposite
of where most effort goes: people write the description and leave the parameter
as a string.

Two rows deserve their own explanation, because each teaches something the
totals hide.

**The opaque schema did not make wrong calls. It made no calls.** With a tool
named `f1` taking `a` and `b`, the model called it 58.3% of the time and,
when it did not, answered from parametric memory instead — inventing a
paragraph about what `ZRG-14` supposedly is. That is a far worse failure than a
malformed call: a wrong call errors, and an invented answer looks like an
answer.

**Without the enum, the model echoes the user's vocabulary into your API.**
Here is the whole of variant B, one row per phrasing:

```text
  MISS  wanted butce     got "bütçe"           ← "ne kadar para ayrildi?"
  MISS  wanted butce     got "mali buyukluk"   ← "mali buyuklugu nedir?"
  OK    wanted personel  got "personel"        ← "kac kisi calisiyor?"
  MISS  wanted personel  got "ekip mevcudu"    ← "ekip mevcudu nedir?"
  OK    wanted sure      got "sure"            ← "kac ay surüyor?"
  MISS  wanted sure      got "takvim"          ← "takvimi ne kadar?"
```

The two it got right are the two where the user's phrasing happened to contain
the API's own word. Everywhere else it passed the question's vocabulary
straight through — *mali buyukluk*, *ekip mevcudu*, *takvim*. The model is not
guessing badly; it has no way to know that your API says `butce`, so it says
what the user said.

And note the first row, which is @sec-turkish-nlp arriving in a new place: the
model wrote **`bütçe`** where the API expects **`butce`**. Correct Turkish,
wrong identifier. Any API whose parameter values are ASCII-folded versions of
real words has this failure waiting in it, and an enum removes it entirely.

::: {.column-margin}
The honest scope: one model, one tool, three fields. What generalises is the
*ordering* — constraints beat prose — not the exact numbers. A larger model
might infer `butce` from context; a schema with twelve fields would make the
enum matter more, not less. Run the variant sweep on your own tools; it is an
afternoon and it is the highest-yield afternoon in this chapter.
:::

::: {.anlp-widget}

### So write schemas in this order

1. **Enumerate everything enumerable.** Every parameter with a fixed value set
   becomes an `enum`. This is the change with the measured effect.
2. **Name the tool for when it applies**, not for what it wraps. `find_orders`
   over `db_query_orders`.
3. **Write the parameter description as a mapping**, from the words users use
   to the value your API wants: *butce = the money allocated*.
4. **Then** write the tool description, for the cases the name leaves open —
   including what the tool is *not* for, which is the part that stops a model
   reaching for it wrongly.
5. **Make optional parameters rare.** Every optional parameter is a decision
   the model has to make with no information, and a default you did not
   document is a guess it will make differently each time.

## Error messages are prompts {#sec-tool-design-errors}

@sec-agent-anatomy's line 6 turned an exception into an observation. That makes
the error string prompt text too — the model reads it and decides what to do
next — and almost nobody writes it that way, because error messages are written
for a human who will be reading a log.

The claim is testable. Hold everything fixed and change only what the tool
returns when it fails. To make every condition face exactly the same failure,
the first tool call is rejected **unconditionally**, whatever the model asked
for; the score is on the *second* call.

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 60 tasks, first call always rejected, four error styles

 error style     retried  valid field  right field   gave up
 bare              23.3%         1.7%         1.7%     76.7%
 traceback         15.0%        11.7%        11.7%     81.7%
 vague             36.7%         3.3%         3.3%     63.3%
 actionable       100.0%       100.0%       100.0%      0.0%
```

The four strings were:

```text
 bare        "Error"

 traceback   Traceback (most recent call last):
               File "server.py", line 118, in veri_getir
                 return RECORDS[proje][alan]
             KeyError: 'bütçe'

 vague       "HATA: gecersiz alan adi."

 actionable  "HATA: 'bütçe' gecerli bir alan degil.
              Gecerli alanlar sunlardir: butce, personel, sure."
```

[One sentence took recovery from 1.7% to 100%.]{.hl} Not a model change, not a
prompt change, not a retry policy — a different string returned by a function.

Three things in that table are worth taking seriously.

**The stack trace is the worst of the four.** It is also the one your tools
almost certainly return today, because it is what happens if you do nothing.
Worse than a bare `"Error"`: 81.7% gave up against 76.7%. A traceback is dense,
authoritative-looking, and contains no statement of what would have worked, so
it reads as *this is broken* rather than *try this instead*. Structured
uselessness is not better than plain uselessness.

**Giving up is the dominant failure, not looping.** Three of the four styles
produced abandonment in the majority of cases — the model stopped calling tools
and answered without the data. That is worse than a retry loop, which at least
announces itself in the transcript. @sec-agent-anatomy found the opposite
failure, an agent that would not stop; here the same architecture will not
*continue*, and the deciding factor is a sentence.

**"Invalid" is barely better than nothing.** The `vague` style names the
problem in words and still recovered 3.3% of the time. Saying that something is
wrong is not the useful part. Saying what would be right is.

### The rule this gives you

An error message a model can use has three parts, and the last one is the one
that matters:

```text
  1. what failed        'bütçe' is not a valid field
  2. why                (optional; often unnecessary)
  3. what would work    valid fields are: butce, personel, sure
```

Write the third part and the rest is optional. Omit it and you have written a
log line, not a tool.

Two corollaries worth building in:

- **Enumerate the valid options in the error**, exactly as you would in an
  enum. If the set is too large to list, list the nearest few — `did you mean
  butce?` is a complete recovery instruction.
- **Never return a raw exception.** Catch it, and translate. The translation is
  a one-line function and, on this evidence, it is worth more than any other
  single change you can make to a tool.

## What a tool returns is part of its design {#sec-tool-design-results}

A tool's return value goes straight into the transcript, which
@sec-agent-anatomy established *is* the agent's state. So a return value is not
output — it is a write to shared memory that every subsequent step will read
and pay for.

Three rules follow, and all three are routinely broken by tools that were
written for humans first.

**A tool that returns 50,000 tokens has broken the agent**, not merely slowed
it. It has consumed context that later steps needed, pushed earlier
observations toward the middle where they are used less well, and multiplied
the cost of every remaining model call. Return what the *task* needs: the
three fields, not the whole record; the matching rows, not the table.

**Paginate, and say so in the result.** `"showing 10 of 247 matches; call again
with offset=10 for more"` is a sentence the model can act on. Silently
truncating to ten is a tool that lies, and the model has no way to find out.

**Summarise on the tool side when the raw form is unusable.** A tool that
wraps a 40-page PDF should not return 40 pages. What it returns is a design
decision about what the agent is for, and making it inside the tool keeps it
out of every prompt that uses the tool.

### Actions need different semantics from lookups

Everything above is about reading. Tools that *do* things need three
properties that read-only tools can ignore, and the cheapest time to add them
is before the first incident.

| property | why an agent specifically needs it |
|:--|:--|
| **Idempotent** | the loop will retry. A step cap, a timeout, or a model that did not see the result will all produce a second call — and "create the invoice" must not create two |
| **Dry-run mode** | lets the agent, or you, see the effect before committing to it. A first-class `dry_run: true` parameter is worth more than any amount of prompt instruction |
| **Confirmation-gated** | some actions should not execute on a model's say-so at all. That gate belongs in the runtime, not the prompt — @sec-guardrails is where this becomes a chapter |

: Three properties read-only tools can skip {tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

The general principle is @sec-agent-anatomy's, restated for the tool author:
the model emits arguments and the runtime decides. Anything you would not let
an unreviewed pull request do automatically, do not let a tool call do
automatically.

## Scaling past fifty tools {#sec-tool-design-scale}

Every tool definition sits in the context of every call, so a flat list of
fifty tools is a large fixed tax on every step, paid whether or not any of them
is relevant. It also gets *less* accurate: more near-duplicate options means
more chances to pick a neighbouring one.

Three ways out, in increasing order of how much they change your architecture:

- **Namespace and prune.** Most large tool surfaces contain three tools that do
  the same thing for historical reasons. Merging them is free accuracy.
- **Search, then load** —
  [**progressive disclosure**](#gloss-progressive-disclosure){#term-progressive-disclosure .term-ref}.
  Expose one `find_tools(query)` and load only the matching definitions for
  that step. This is @sec-retrieval applied to your
  own API surface, and it is the standard answer above roughly fifty tools.
- **Give it an interpreter instead.** If your tools are mostly small
  transformations, a sandboxed code environment replaces fifty definitions
  with one — the model composes what it needs rather than picking from a menu.

::: {#gloss-progressive-disclosure .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Progressive disclosure** — loading only the tool definitions relevant to the
current step instead of all of them, so a large surface does not tax every
call. [↩](#term-progressive-disclosure){.term-back}
:::

### Code mode, and what it costs

That third option — [**code mode**](#gloss-code-mode){#term-code-mode .term-ref}
— deserves naming clearly, because it is increasingly the default in serious
systems.

::: {#gloss-code-mode .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Code mode** — giving an agent a sandboxed interpreter instead of a fixed
tool list. Composition, loops and intermediate variables come free; a readable
whitelist does not. [↩](#term-code-mode){.term-back}
::: Instead of `filter_rows`, `sum_column` and
`join_tables`, you expose a sandbox and let the model write the composition.
It is genuinely more expressive: composition, loops and intermediate variables
come free, and they are exactly what a fixed tool list makes awkward.

The cost is that [you have replaced a whitelist with an interpreter]{.hl}. A
tool list is a security boundary you can read; a sandbox is a security boundary
you have to build and keep believing in. That is a real trade and it belongs to
@sec-agent-security rather than to a paragraph here — but the design decision
is made in this chapter, when you choose what surface to expose.

## Evaluating a tool {#sec-tool-design-eval}

A tool is not correct because it works. It is correct when **the model calls it
right**, which is a property of the pair and can only be measured by asking.

The evaluation is small enough to build in an afternoon and it is the same
shape as this chapter's two experiments:

1. **Collect twenty real requests** that should reach this tool, phrased the
   way users phrase them rather than the way your API is named. This is where
   the misuse hides.
2. **Score the call, not the outcome.** Was the right tool chosen; are the
   arguments right? Executing muddles a schema problem with everything
   downstream — the schema experiment above deliberately executed nothing.
3. **Count the three failure kinds separately**, because they have different
   fixes:

| failure | what it means | what fixes it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Not called** | the model answered without the tool, or picked a neighbour | the *name*, and the description's "use this when" |
| **Called wrong** | right tool, wrong arguments | types and enums, then parameter descriptions |
| **Not recovered** | a failed call the model could not act on | the error string |

: Three failure kinds, three different fixes {tbl-colwidths="[20,44,36]"}

4. **Add the twenty requests to your regression set.** A tool description is
   prompt text, so changing it is a change to system behaviour and deserves the
   same treatment as changing a prompt — @sec-llm-eval sized how many items you
   need before a difference means anything.

The "not called" row is the one worth instrumenting in production, because it
is invisible otherwise. A tool that is never selected produces no errors and no
logs; it just quietly does not participate, while the model answers from memory
— which is exactly what the opaque schema did, 41.7% of the time, in prose that
looked like an answer.

## Lab: fix a tool by measuring it {#sec-tool-design-lab}

### Step 1 — pick a tool the model gets wrong

If you do not know which one, you have found the first task: log tool calls
with their arguments for a day.

### Step 2 — write twenty requests in users' words

Not in your API's words. The gap between the two is the thing being measured.

### Step 3 — score the call, executing nothing

Right tool, right arguments, both or neither. Record the baseline.

### Step 4 — change one thing: add enums

Every parameter with a fixed value set. Re-measure. On this chapter's tool that
single change was worth 75 points.

### Step 5 — now rewrite the descriptions

Re-measure again. Report the delta honestly, including if it is zero, as it was
here.

### Step 6 — break it on purpose and fix the error string

Force a failing call. Try the bare error, then the actionable one. Count how
often the model recovers.

### What to hand in

The four-row table of your own — baseline, enums, descriptions, error string —
and one sentence saying which change you would have predicted was largest, and
whether you were right.

## Intuition checks {#sec-tool-design-intuition}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Where should you spend your time on a tool schema?

On enums, before prose. Measured here, moving one parameter from a free string
to an enumerated list took correct calls from **25% to 100%**, and adding
careful descriptions on top added nothing measurable. Constraints make wrong
calls unrepresentable; descriptions only make them less likely, and the model
has no way to check whether it guessed your vocabulary right.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your tool has a badly named, undocumented schema. What is the failure?

Usually not a wrong call — **no call**. With an opaque schema the model here
invoked the tool only 58.3% of the time and otherwise answered from parametric
memory, producing a confident paragraph about something it could not know. A
wrong call raises an error you can see; an unused tool produces a plausible
answer and no signal at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why does a model pass "mali buyukluk" where your API wants "butce"?

Because nothing told it otherwise, so it echoes the user's vocabulary into your
parameter. In this chapter's measurement the only phrasings that worked were
the two where the user's words happened to contain the API's own word. One case
is worth noticing specially: the model wrote `bütçe` where the API expects
`butce` — correct Turkish, wrong identifier, and a failure waiting inside any
API whose values are ASCII-folded words.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. What should a tool return when it fails?

What would have worked. Measured across four styles, recovery went from **1.7%
to 100%** purely by naming the invalid value and listing the valid ones. The
striking row is the stack trace: at **81.7% abandonment** it was worse than a
bare `"Error"`, because it is dense, authoritative, and contains no statement
of what to try instead. Never return a raw exception.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. A tool returns the full record — 8,000 tokens. Is that a problem?

Yes, and it is a problem for the whole run rather than that step. The return
value goes into the transcript, which @sec-agent-anatomy showed *is* the
agent's state, so it is re-sent on every subsequent model call and it crowds
out what later steps need. Return the fields the task needs, paginate with the
pagination stated in the result, and summarise on the tool side when the raw
form is unusable.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When do you stop adding tools and expose an interpreter instead?

When the tools are mostly small transformations that users want to *compose* —
filter, then sum, then join — because composition is exactly what a fixed list
makes awkward and what code makes free. Be explicit about the price: you have
replaced a whitelist you can read with a sandbox you have to build and keep
trusting. That is a security decision made in this chapter and paid for in
@sec-agent-security.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-tool-design-exercises}

1. **The enum sweep.** Take one tool with a free-string parameter that has a
   fixed value set. Measure correct calls, add the enum, measure again. Report
   both numbers.
2. **Users' words, not yours.** Write twenty requests for one of your tools in
   the vocabulary your users actually use. Count how many produce the right
   arguments. The gap is your parameter descriptions' job.
3. **Rewrite the worst error.** Find the ugliest error string a tool of yours
   can return. Rewrite it in the three-part form. Measure recovery before and
   after.
4. **Find the silent tool.** Instrument which tools are never selected. For
   each one, decide whether it is redundant or badly named — both are fixable,
   and both are invisible without the instrumentation.
5. **Budget a return value.** Take a tool that returns a whole record and
   compute what it costs across a ten-step run. Then decide what it should
   return instead.
6. **Dry-run.** Add a `dry_run` parameter to a tool that writes something.
   Measure whether the agent uses it when asked to be careful, and whether the
   instruction is even necessary once the parameter exists.
7. **The ASCII trap.** If your API uses ASCII-folded identifiers derived from
   words in a language with diacritics, write the test that catches
   `bütçe`/`butce` before a user does.

## Interview questions {#sec-tool-design-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.**
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: What makes a good tool schema?**

Start from the framing that decides everything else: the schema is prompt text,
not documentation, because the model gets one shot from it with no way to check.
Then order the work by effect. Enums first — measured here, enumerating one
parameter took correct calls from 25% to 100% while prose descriptions on top
added nothing. Then a name that says *when* the tool applies. Then parameter
descriptions written as a mapping from users' words to your API's words,
because otherwise the model passes the user's vocabulary straight through.

**Q: Your agent ignores a tool that would answer the question. Why?**

Most likely the name and description do not say when it applies, so the model
does not recognise the situation as this tool's. The important half of the
answer is what that failure looks like: not an error, but an answer from
parametric memory. In this chapter's measurement an opaque schema went uncalled
41.7% of the time and produced confident invented prose instead. So instrument
*selection*, not just failures.

**Q: What should a tool return on error?**

A sentence saying what would have worked, with the valid options enumerated.
Measured across four styles, that took recovery from 1.7% to 100%. And say the
counterintuitive part, because it is the useful one: a stack trace was the
*worst* of the four — worse than a bare "Error" — because it looks
authoritative and contains no path forward. Catch the exception and translate
it.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: How do you evaluate a tool?**

By whether the model calls it correctly, which is a property of the pair. Twenty
requests in users' phrasing, scored on the emitted call rather than the outcome
so a schema problem is not confounded with everything downstream, bucketed into
not-called, called-wrong and not-recovered — because those have three different
fixes. Then keep the twenty in the regression set, since a description change is
a behaviour change.

**Q: You have eighty tools and accuracy is falling. What do you do?**

First merge and prune, because large surfaces accumulate near-duplicates and
every extra near-neighbour is another chance to pick the wrong one. Then move
from a flat list to search-then-load, so only the relevant definitions occupy
the context — @sec-retrieval applied to your own API. If the tools are mostly
small composable transformations, consider replacing them with a sandboxed
interpreter, and be explicit that you are trading a readable whitelist for a
security boundary you now have to maintain.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-tool-design-deeper}

Do this before reading anything: take one tool, add enums to every parameter
that has a fixed value set, and measure the change. It is twenty minutes.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [Writing tools for agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) — Anthropic | the closest thing to a specification for this chapter's subject, from people who watch tool misuse at scale |
| [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic | the surrounding argument: what to build before you need tools at all |
| [`pydantic-ai`](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) | tools as typed functions, with validation errors that are already model-readable — the error-message finding, built in |
| [`outlines`](https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines) | @sec-decoding's constrained generation, which is the mechanism that makes an enum a guarantee rather than a suggestion |
| [`smolagents`](https://github.com/huggingface/smolagents) | includes code-mode agents, so you can compare the two surfaces on your own task |
| [JSON Schema documentation](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema) | the constraint vocabulary you are actually writing in; most people use a tenth of it |

## What to remember {#sec-tool-design-summary}

- **A tool schema is prompt text, not documentation.** The model gets one shot
  from it, cannot read your source, and cannot check a guess. Whatever the
  schema does not say, it invents.
- **Enums do the work; prose does not.** Moving one parameter from a free
  string to an enumerated list took correct calls from **25% to 100%**, and
  adding careful descriptions on top added **nothing measurable**. Spend the
  time where the measurement is.
- **A bad schema produces no call, not a wrong call.** The opaque variant went
  uncalled **41.7%** of the time and answered from parametric memory instead —
  a confident invented paragraph, which is worse than an error because it looks
  like an answer.
- **Without constraints the model echoes the user's vocabulary into your API.**
  *mali buyukluk*, *ekip mevcudu*, *takvim* — and `bütçe` where the API wanted
  `butce`, which is @sec-turkish-nlp's problem arriving inside a function
  signature.
- **The error string is worth more than any other single change.** Recovery
  went from **1.7% to 100%** by naming the invalid value and listing the valid
  ones. Write what *would* have worked; the rest is optional.
- **A stack trace is worse than nothing.** At **81.7% abandonment** it beat a
  bare `"Error"` for uselessness, because it looks authoritative and offers no
  path forward. Catch and translate.
- **The dominant failure after an error is giving up, not looping.** Three of
  four error styles made the model stop calling tools and answer without the
  data — a quieter failure than a retry loop and a worse one.
- **What a tool returns is a write to the agent's state.** Return the fields
  the task needs, state the pagination in the result, and summarise on the tool
  side. A tool that returns 50,000 tokens has not slowed the agent down; it has
  taken the context later steps needed.
